standard_text: Momentum (p = mv); impulse; the conservation of momentum; elastic and inelastic collisions; safety devices. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 10, Quarter 2: Force, Motion, and Energy)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Force, Motion, and Energy): momentum and impulse, momentum and impulse problems, collisions, momentum problems and impulse and safety. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: In an isolated system the total momentum is conserved.
body_html:
How to think about it

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv; it is a vector, so choose a positive direction. Newton's second law can be written as Fnet = Δp/Δt: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum.

In an isolated system (no external resultant force) the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after it. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; in an inelastic collision it is not. Impulse FnetΔt = Δp: airbags, crumple zones and arrestor beds increase Δt, which reduces the force.

Example

A 2 kg ball at 3 m·s⁻¹. Momentum?

p = mv

Answer: 6 kg·m·s⁻¹

Example

A 1 kg cart at 4 m·s⁻¹ joins a 1 kg cart at rest. Common velocity?

Total p = 4

Answer: 2 m·s⁻¹

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that momentum has a direction.
  • Thinking kinetic energy is conserved in every collision.
  • Thinking an airbag reduces the change in momentum.

faq.q: How does an airbag reduce injury?
faq.a: It increases the time over which the momentum changes, so the force on the passenger is smaller.

items.q: A 5 kg bowling ball moving at 3 m/s stops in 0.4 s. What average force acts on it?
